The key elements are: (1) black-box jailbreak, (2) universality across harmful intents, (3) generating a large/endless supply of diverse attack prompts (not a fixed set).

Paper [4] (h4rm3l) explicitly addresses the problem of "fail to cover sufficiently large and diverse sets of jailbreak attacks" and proposes composable synthesis to generate many attack variants. Paper [8] proposes novel cipher-based jailbreaks. Paper [15] (TAP) is a black-box automated jailbreak generator. Paper [25] uses random search with multiple restarts to generate attack prompts.

Paper [4] is closest — it explicitly targets the problem of generating large, diverse sets of jailbreak attacks (not a fixed hand-crafted set), which is substantively equivalent to the purpose of generating an endless supply. Paper [15] also generates jailbreaks automatically in a black-box setting. However, neither specifically frames the purpose as "endless supply via random sampling of encodings for a single harmful intent." Paper [4]'s purpose is "composable synthesis to cover large/diverse attack space," which is substantively equivalent at the problem-class level.

Paper [8] also targets the purpose of creating novel cipher-based jailbreaks that bypass safety training, which partially overlaps. But the "endless supply via random encoding" framing is most closely matched by [4].

I'll call this COVERED by [4] (and partially [15]).

**MECHANISM: Bijection learning — teach the target LLM an arbitrary randomly-generated string-to-string encoding in-context, pass encoded harmful query, apply inverse mapping + denoiser to recover response; random sampling of encodings enables best-of-n.**

Key primitives: (a) in-context teaching of a custom encoding/cipher to the LLM, (b) encoding the harmful query in that cipher, (c) random generation of the encoding, (d) best-of-n over many random encodings, (e) denoiser for decoding errors.

Paper [8] ("When Competency in Reasoning Opens the Door to Vulnerability") explicitly uses "novel complex ciphers" and "user-defined ciphers" taught in-context to jailbreak LLMs — "Enhanced reasoning enables LLMs to interpret complex instructions and decode complex user-defined ciphers." This is substantively the same primitive: teach the LLM a custom cipher in-context, encode the harmful query. The random generation and best-of-n are additional elements.

Paper [25] uses random search with multiple restarts (best-of-n flavor) on adversarial suffixes, but the encoding mechanism differs.

Paper [6] uses in-context demonstrations to modulate safety alignment, but not cipher-based encoding.

The core primitive — in-context teaching of a user-defined cipher/encoding to bypass safety — is clearly present in [8]. The random sampling + best-of-n is a natural extension (similar to [25]'s random restarts). The denoiser is a minor engineering addition.

This is COVERED by [8] (core cipher-in-context primitive) and partially [25] (random restarts/best-of-n).

AdvBench and HarmBench are named benchmark families used extensively in jailbreak literature. Papers [1], [4], [5], [8], [15], [21], [25] all evaluate jailbreak attacks using ASR metrics on AdvBench or HarmBench against frontier models. This is COVERED by [21] and [25] (HarmBench, ASR against frontier models).
